name: פונקציה סתומה – נגזרות חלקיות של g על משטח ריבועי (באנגלית)
questiontext:
Finally, one review question on the implicit function theory, unrelated to vector fields and path integrals:

Consider the set of all the solutions in \(R^3\) to the following equation

\[M = \left \{{{CT:0}} \in R^3 \ | \ {{CT:1}} = {{CT:2}} \right \} \]

By the implicit function theorem, in a small enough neighbourhood of the point \(p= {{CT:0}} = {{CT:3}} \in R^3\), it is possible to express the collection of points \(M\) as a graph of a function \({{CT:4}}=g ({{CT:5}},{{CT:6}})\). Namely \({{CT:0}} \in M {\text{ if and only if }} {{CT:4}}=g ({{CT:5}},{{CT:6}}).\)

Before continuing with the question please make sure that indeed \(p \in M\) and that the conditions of the implicit function theorem are indeed satisfied here!

Now use the implicit function theorem in order to calculate the partial derivatives of the function \({{CT:4}}({{CT:5}},{{CT:6}})\) at the relevant point.

\(\frac{\partial g}{\partial {{CT:5}}} ({{CT:7}},{{CT:8}}) \) = [[input:ans1]]
[[validation:ans1]]
\(\frac{\partial g}{\partial {{CT:6}}} ({{CT:7}},{{CT:8}}) \) = [[input:ans2]]
[[validation:ans2]]
generalfeedback:
Outline: Check that \(p\) lies on the surface and that the partial derivative of \(F\) with respect to \({{CT:4}}\) is nonzero there, then use \(g_{ {{CT:5}} }=-F_{ {{CT:5}} }/F_{ {{CT:4}} }\) (and the same for \({{CT:6}}\)).
Step 1 — The point lies on \(M\)
Let \(F(x,y,z)={{CT:1}}-{{CT:2}}\), so that \(M\) is the zero set of \(F\). Substitute the point \(p=({{CT:9}},{{CT:10}},{{CT:11}})\):

\[ f({{CT:9}},{{CT:10}},{{CT:11}})={{CT:2}} \]

hence \(F(p)=0\), that is, \(p\in M\).
Step 2 — The partial derivatives
The partial derivatives of \(F\) (the constant \({{CT:2}}\) disappears):

\[ F_x={{CT:12}} \]

\[ F_y={{CT:13}} \]

\[ F_z={{CT:14}} \]

and at the point \(p\):

\[ F_x(p)={{CT:15}},\qquad F_y(p)={{CT:16}},\qquad F_z(p)={{CT:17}} \]

Step 3 — The conditions of the implicit function theorem
The partial derivatives of \(F\) are continuous near \(p\), and \(F(p)=0\). The variable to be expressed is \({{CT:4}}\), and \(F_{ {{CT:4}} }(p)={{CT:18}}\neq 0\). So by the theorem, near \(p\) we have \({{CT:4}}=g({{CT:5}},{{CT:6}})\) with \(g\) differentiable.
Step 4 — The partial derivatives of g
Differentiating the identity \(F\big(\ldots,g({{CT:5}},{{CT:6}}),\ldots\big)=0\) with respect to \({{CT:5}}\) and to \({{CT:6}}\) gives \(F_{ {{CT:5}} }+F_{ {{CT:4}} }\,g_{ {{CT:5}} }=0\) and \(F_{ {{CT:6}} }+F_{ {{CT:4}} }\,g_{ {{CT:6}} }=0\). Hence at \(({{CT:5}},{{CT:6}})=({{CT:7}},{{CT:8}})\):

\[ \frac{\partial g}{\partial {{CT:5}}}({{CT:7}},{{CT:8}})=-\frac{F_{ {{CT:5}} }(p)}{F_{ {{CT:4}} }(p)}=-\frac{ {{CT:19}} }{ {{CT:18}} }={{CT:20}} \]

\[ \frac{\partial g}{\partial {{CT:6}}}({{CT:7}},{{CT:8}})=-\frac{F_{ {{CT:6}} }(p)}{F_{ {{CT:4}} }(p)}=-\frac{ {{CT:21}} }{ {{CT:18}} }={{CT:22}} \]
